questions.stem: What is habitat fragmentation?
options: Removing every plant from an area so that only bare soil is left
Adding excess nutrients to a waterway from farm fertilisers
Introducing a species into an area where it did not occur
Breaking a continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches
questions.explanation: Fragmentation splits habitat into patches separated by farmland, roads or towns. Clearing all vegetation is habitat destruction, and adding nutrients leads to eutrophication.

questions.stem: Why are small, isolated habitat fragments a threat to the populations living in them?
options: Fragments receive more rainfall, so the soil becomes too wet for most species
Populations are small and cut off, so gene flow falls and local extinction is likely
Fragments always contain more predators than an equal area of continuous native habitat
Animals in fragments grow larger, so they need more food than is available
questions.explanation: Small, isolated populations lose genetic diversity through drift and inbreeding and can be wiped out by a single fire or disease, with no migrants to recolonise. Wildlife corridors linking fragments help restore gene flow.

questions.stem: How can a vegetation corridor linking two bushland fragments help conservation?
options: It stops all of the predators from entering either of the fragments
It keeps the two populations apart so each becomes a species
It removes the need to control any introduced species nearby
Animals can move between the fragments, maintaining gene flow
questions.explanation: Corridors let individuals disperse between patches, increasing the effective population size and gene flow and allowing recolonisation after local extinctions. They do not keep out predators.

questions.stem: How does clearing native vegetation lead to soil erosion?
options: Without roots and cover, soil becomes heavier and sinks below the surface
Clearing adds salt to the soil, which dissolves the soil particles
Clearing raises soil temperature, which turns the soil into rock
Without roots and cover, soil is easily carried away by wind and water
questions.explanation: Plant roots bind soil and plant cover protects it from wind and rain, so cleared land loses topsoil quickly. Eroded soil can also smother aquatic habitats downstream.

questions.stem: In the WA wheatbelt, deep-rooted native vegetation was replaced by shallow-rooted annual crops. Why did large areas then become salt-affected?
options: Farmers irrigated with seawater, which left salt behind as it evaporated
Native plants had absorbed salt from rain, so salt now falls straight onto soil
Less water was used by plants, so the water table rose and brought salt to the surface
Crops release salt from their roots, and the salt builds up in the soil over many years
questions.explanation: Native trees and shrubs used most of the rainfall; annual crops use less, so more water reaches the groundwater and the water table rises, dissolving stored salts and carrying them into the root zone. This is dryland salinity.

questions.stem: Which strategy is most likely to reduce dryland salinity in a catchment?
options: Clearing the remaining trees so that more of the rain reaches the soil
Replacing perennial pastures with more shallow-rooted crops
Adding fertiliser so that crops grow faster in salty soil
Planting deep-rooted perennial vegetation to lower the water table
questions.explanation: Deep-rooted perennials such as trees and saltbush use more water year-round, which helps keep the water table below the root zone. Further clearing would raise the water table and worsen salinity.

questions.stem: Why do many introduced species become invasive in Australia?
options: They often lack natural predators, competitors and diseases here
They are always larger than every native species that they meet
They cannot reproduce, so they live much longer than natives
They eat only other introduced species, so they spread freely
questions.explanation: Freed from the predators, competitors and pathogens that limited them in their native range, introduced species can increase rapidly. Native species may also lack defences against them.

questions.stem: How have European red foxes and feral cats affected native Australian mammals?
options: By spreading the chytrid fungus that has killed many native mammals
By preying heavily on small and medium-sized mammals that lacked defences
By competing with eucalypts for water in the dry inland regions
By pollinating native plants, so that native grazing mammals have more food
questions.explanation: Foxes and cats are efficient introduced predators, and many small to medium-sized native mammals evolved without them, so populations declined or disappeared. Chytrid fungus affects amphibians, not mammals.

questions.stem: Why have cane toads caused declines in predators such as northern quolls and some goannas?
options: The toads compete with the predators for nesting sites in tree hollows
The toads are toxic, and predators that eat them are often poisoned
The toads eat the predators' eggs, so few young survive to adulthood
The toads carry a virus that spreads rapidly through these predators
questions.explanation: Cane toads produce toxins in their skin glands, and native predators that have not evolved with them often die after eating a toad. The decline is due to poisoning, not disease or competition.

questions.stem: Baits containing 1080 (sodium fluoroacetate) are used in WA to control foxes, yet many native WA mammals are relatively tolerant of it. What explains this?
options: Native mammals avoid all meat, so they never eat any of the baits laid
1080 affects only animals introduced to Australia after 1788
Native mammals are immunised against 1080 before baiting starts
Some native WA plants contain it, so native animals evolved tolerance
questions.explanation: Fluoroacetate occurs naturally in some native WA plants, such as Gastrolobium species, so many native animals that evolved alongside them are tolerant, while foxes and cats are highly susceptible. This allows baiting to target introduced predators.

questions.stem: Rabbits graze native pastures and seedlings heavily. Which combination of effects on native ecosystems is most likely?
options: Fewer foxes and cats, because rabbits outcompete them for prey
Less erosion, because rabbit burrows hold the topsoil in place
Competition with native herbivores, loss of seedlings and more erosion
More native seedlings grow, because rabbit droppings fertilise the soil
questions.explanation: Rabbits compete with native herbivores for food, prevent plant regeneration by eating seedlings, and strip ground cover, which increases erosion. They also support larger populations of introduced predators.

questions.stem: Which is an example of unsustainable use of a natural resource?
options: Rotating grazing so that pastures have time to recover
Catching fish faster than the population can replace itself
Setting catch limits based on surveys of fish population size
Closing a fishery during the breeding season each year
questions.explanation: Use is unsustainable when a resource is harvested faster than it can regenerate, leading to collapse. Catch limits, seasonal closures and rotation are management strategies to keep use sustainable.

questions.stem: A fish population was harvested at a steady rate for decades, but its numbers and the average size of fish caught both fell. What is the best interpretation?
options: The fish evolved to grow larger to avoid being caught by nets
Harvesting had no effect, because fish populations never decline
Harvesting exceeded the rate of replacement, removing breeding adults
The fish population grew too large and ran out of food in the sea
questions.explanation: Falling numbers and smaller fish show that large breeding adults are being removed faster than young fish can grow and replace them. Fewer breeders means fewer young, so the decline accelerates unless harvesting is reduced.

questions.stem: What is biomagnification?
options: The spread of an introduced species through a new ecosystem
The release of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels
A persistent chemical's concentration increasing at each trophic level
The rapid growth of algae in water enriched with nitrates and phosphates
questions.explanation: Persistent, fat-soluble chemicals such as DDT and mercury are stored in tissues rather than excreted, so they become more concentrated at each step up a food chain. Algal growth from nutrients is eutrophication.

questions.stem: A pesticide in a lake is 0.02 parts per million (ppm) in the water, 5 ppm in small fish and 75 ppm in a fish-eating bird. Why is the concentration highest in the bird?
options: The bird drinks more lake water than the fish, so it absorbs more pesticide
The bird breaks the pesticide down into larger, more toxic molecules
The fish excrete the pesticide straight into the bird's food supply
Each bird eats many fish over its life and stores the persistent chemical
questions.explanation: Top predators eat many prey, each carrying a stored dose of the chemical, and they cannot excrete it, so it accumulates. This is why birds of prey were among the species most harmed by DDT.

questions.stem: Which property makes a pollutant most likely to biomagnify?
options: It is water-soluble, so it is quickly excreted from the body in urine
It breaks down within hours once it enters the environment
It is broken down by decomposers into harmless nutrients
It is persistent and fat-soluble, so it is stored in body tissues
questions.explanation: A chemical that resists breakdown and dissolves in fat stays in the body and is passed on when the organism is eaten. Water-soluble or rapidly degraded chemicals do not build up along food chains.

questions.stem: Fertiliser runs off farmland into an estuary. Which sequence describes eutrophication?
options: Nutrients rise, algae bloom, algae die, decomposers use up oxygen, fish die
Nutrients rise, oxygen rises, algae die, decomposers die, fish numbers rise
Algae die, nutrients fall, oxygen rises, decomposers grow, fish numbers rise
Oxygen falls, nutrients fall, algae bloom, decomposers die, fish numbers rise
questions.explanation: Excess nitrates and phosphates fuel rapid algal growth; when the algae die, decomposers break them down and use up dissolved oxygen, so fish and other animals suffocate. Reducing nutrient run-off is the main remedy.

questions.stem: Dissolved oxygen in a lake is lowest a few weeks after an algal bloom, not during it. What explains the delay?
options: Algae absorb oxygen during the bloom and release it as they die
Dead algae release nitrogen gas, which pushes oxygen out of the water
Oxygen falls when decomposers respire as they break down the dead algae
Living algae use more oxygen in photosynthesis than they release
questions.explanation: While the bloom is alive it photosynthesises and adds oxygen by day; when the algae die, the large mass of dead matter fuels decomposer respiration, which consumes oxygen. Photosynthesis releases oxygen rather than using it.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: The cooling of Earth as more sunlight is reflected by polluted clouds
Extra warming as human emissions add greenhouse gases to the atmosphere
The natural warming that keeps Earth habitable, without human influence
The thinning of the ozone layer by chemicals released from aerosol cans
questions.explanation: Human activities such as burning fossil fuels and clearing land raise levels of gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, which trap more heat. The natural greenhouse effect existed before human emissions.

questions.stem: Which is an expected effect of climate change on biodiversity?
options: Species stop evolving, because the climate no longer changes their environment
Species ranges shift as temperatures rise, and some species cannot move fast enough
Every species becomes more abundant, because warmer conditions favour all of their growth
Coral reefs grow faster, because corals need warmer and more acidic water
questions.explanation: As conditions change, many species shift towards the poles or uphill; those with limited dispersal or nowhere to go, such as mountain-top species, may decline. Warmer, more acidic seas cause coral bleaching rather than faster growth.

questions.stem: Which is a genetic conservation strategy?
options: Replanting native species on cleared farmland
Storing seeds of threatened plants in a seed bank
Fencing a reserve to exclude foxes and feral cats
Closing a marine area to recreational fishing
questions.explanation: Gene and seed banks, and captive breeding programs, preserve genetic material and diversity. Fencing and revegetation are environmental strategies, and closing an area to fishing is a management strategy.

questions.stem: Perth Zoo breeds the critically endangered western swamp tortoise and releases young into protected wetlands. Which type of conservation strategy is the breeding program?
options: Genetic: a captive breeding program
Environmental: control of introduced species
Management: restricted recreational access
Environmental: revegetation of habitat
questions.explanation: Captive breeding maintains and increases the population and its genetic diversity, so it is a genetic strategy. Protecting the release wetlands would involve environmental and management strategies.

questions.stem: Why should a captive breeding program for a threatened species start with founders from as many wild populations as possible?
options: To reduce the number of alleles present in the program
To capture as much of the species' genetic diversity as possible
To make all of the released animals genetically identical
To ensure the founders are as closely related as possible
questions.explanation: Founders from several populations carry a wider range of alleles, reducing inbreeding and giving released animals more capacity to adapt. A program started from a few related animals has low diversity from the outset.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental conservation strategy?
options: Freezing sperm and eggs of threatened animals
Breeding threatened animals in a zoo
Storing seeds in a seed bank
Revegetating cleared land with local native plants
questions.explanation: Environmental strategies repair or protect habitat, for example revegetation and control of introduced species. Freezing gametes, captive breeding and seed banks are genetic strategies.

questions.stem: A marine park has sanctuary zones where all fishing is banned and other zones where recreational fishing is allowed with bag limits. Which type of conservation strategy is this?
options: Genetic: captive breeding of the fish species
Management: protected areas with restricted access
Genetic: storing genes from marine species
Environmental: revegetation of the sea floor
questions.explanation: Protected areas and limits on commercial and recreational use are management strategies. They allow populations inside sanctuary zones to recover, which can also benefit surrounding areas.

questions.stem: A threatened marsupial lives only in one reserve, where foxes are its main threat. Which combination of strategies gives the best long-term protection?
options: Captive breeding only, with all animals kept permanently in zoos
A seed bank of the reserve's plants, with no action on foxes
Opening the reserve to more visitors to raise awareness
Fox control in the reserve plus a captive insurance population elsewhere
questions.explanation: Controlling foxes tackles the main threat in the wild, while a separate insurance population protects against a catastrophe such as fire in the single reserve. Combining environmental and genetic strategies is stronger than either alone.

questions.stem: When a new marine conservation reserve is planned, which factors must be considered besides biodiversity?
options: Only how many species are found in the area, nothing else
Commercial and recreational uses, and Indigenous Peoples' usage rights
Only the number of tourists who could visit the area each year
Only the views of the commercial fishing companies working in the area
questions.explanation: Identifying and classifying reserve areas requires balancing conservation with commercial and recreational uses of the area and the usage rights of Indigenous Peoples. Considering only one group's interests would not meet these requirements.

questions.stem: Shark Bay and the Great Barrier Reef are examples of which kind of internationally recognised area?
options: Seed banks
Wildlife corridors
World Heritage sites
Biodiversity hotspots
questions.explanation: Both are inscribed on the World Heritage List under an international agreement that encourages countries to protect places of outstanding universal value. South West WA is an example of a biodiversity hotspot.

questions.stem: South West WA is recognised as a biodiversity hotspot. What does this mean?
options: It is a site where new species are deliberately introduced to raise diversity
It has many endemic species and has lost much of its original habitat
It has the highest temperatures recorded anywhere in Australia
It has very few species, so every one of them must be protected
questions.explanation: Biodiversity hotspots are regions with exceptionally high numbers of endemic species, especially plants, that have also lost a large share of their original vegetation. They are priorities for conservation.

questions.stem: Why do species such as migratory shorebirds, humpback whales and marine turtles need international agreements for their protection?
options: They are all invasive species that must be controlled at national borders
They breed only in captivity, so zoos in many countries must cooperate
They cross many countries' areas, so protection in one place is not enough
They are found in only one country, so other countries must pay for them
questions.explanation: Migratory species depend on breeding, feeding and resting sites along routes that span several countries, so losses anywhere on the route affect the whole population. International cooperation protects these sites and routes.

questions.stem: How do satellite sensing and remote monitoring help conservation?
options: They remove the need for any field surveys to check what is on the ground
They track changes in habitat and animal movements over large areas and long periods
They prevent land clearing directly, by blocking machinery from reaching the bushland
They increase the genetic diversity of populations that are being monitored
questions.explanation: Satellite images can reveal clearing, fire scars and changes in vegetation over time, and satellite tags track animals across oceans and continents. Field data are still needed to confirm and interpret what is seen remotely.

questions.stem: Satellite tags on whale sharks at Ningaloo show some travel thousands of kilometres into other nations' waters. What is the main conservation implication?
options: Protection at Ningaloo alone cannot secure the population's survival
Whale sharks should be kept permanently at Ningaloo to protect them
The Ningaloo population is a separate species from all other whale sharks
Satellite tagging proves that whale sharks face no threats elsewhere
questions.explanation: Animals that migrate across borders face threats along their whole route, so international cooperation is needed alongside local protection. Tagging data show movements; they do not show the absence of threats.

questions.stem: Why is the use of keystone species theory in conservation debated?
options: Keystone species are always introduced, so they should be removed, not protected
Keystone species theory has never been tested with any field observations
Protecting one species may not be enough to keep a complex ecosystem working
Keystone species have no effect on other species, so protecting them is wasted
questions.explanation: Protecting a keystone species can benefit many others, but some scientists argue that ecosystems depend on many interacting species and processes, so single-species approaches may miss important threats. This is a genuine scientific debate.

questions.stem: What is a seed bank used for in conservation?
options: Storing seeds so plants can be regrown if wild populations are lost
Planting seeds as quickly as possible to cover cleared farmland
Feeding seeds to captive animals in a breeding program
Selling seeds so that farmers can grow more crops
questions.explanation: Seed banks store seeds under cool, dry conditions so that genetic diversity is preserved and plants can be reintroduced if wild populations decline or are destroyed. They are a genetic conservation strategy.

questions.stem: Which human activity contributes most directly to the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: Using seed banks to store native seeds
Fencing reserves to keep out foxes
Burning coal, oil and gas for energy
Planting trees on cleared farmland
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide stored for millions of years, increasing the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Planting trees removes carbon dioxide rather than adding it.
